title: How effective combined pills are
answer: When combined pills are taken every day without missing any, fewer than 1 in 100 women get pregnant in a year. In real life, when pills are sometimes missed or packs started late, about 7 in 100 women get pregnant in a year. The secret is to take one every day and start each new pack on time. Pills do not protect against HIV or other STIs.

title: The pill and cancer
answer: Using combined pills actually lowers the risk of cancer of the womb lining and of the ovaries, and this protection lasts for years after stopping. Studies on breast cancer and cervical cancer show small or unclear changes in risk while using pills. Overall, the pill is safe for most young people. Ask your health worker if you have worries or a family history of cancer.

answer: Alcohol does not stop the pill from working. title: Smoking and the pill
answer: Smoking while using combined pills raises the risk of blood clots, heart attack and stroke, especially for women aged 35 and older. Young women who smoke can usually use combined pills, but stopping smoking is best for your health. Tell your health worker if you smoke; they may suggest a progestin-only pill or another method.

title: What progestin-only pills are
answer: Progestin-only pills, sometimes called mini-pills, contain only one hormone, a progestin, and no estrogen. They work mainly by thickening the mucus at the cervix so sperm cannot pass, and in some users by stopping eggs being released. They are taken every day with no break. They are often chosen by breastfeeding women and people who cannot use estrogen.
